title: Head of government
description: Chief officer of the executive branch of a government
wiki_lead:
The head of government serves as the highest official in the executive branch of a state. The head of government usually handles the day to day affairs of the state, and leads the ministers who control the government. In many democratic systems the head of state is also the head of government. In non democratic systems the head of government is usually established via military intervention.
In most parliamentary systems, including constitutional monarchies, the head of government is the de facto political leader of the government, and is answerable to at least one chamber of the legislature. Although there is often a formal reporting relationship to a head of state, the latter usually acts as a figurehead who may take the role of chief executive on limited occasions, either when receiving constitutional advice from the head of government or under specific provisions in a constitution.
In semi-presidential systems, the head of government may answer to both the head of state and the legislature with the specifics provided by each country's constitution. 
In communist states, the general secretary of the Communist Party is the supreme leader, serving as de facto head of state and government. In some cases, the general secretary was also the de jure head of government, or Premier, like in the Soviet Union under Joseph Stalin from 1941 to 1953 and Nikita Khrushchev from 1958 to 1964. In other cases, like in modern-day China, the position of Premier is held by a different politician.

In other cases, like in modern-day China, the position of Premier is held by a different politician.


Types
In some governments, those who are the heads of state also perform the duties of the head of government. The President of the United States is one example. Certain governments those roles are separate, with the head of state merely being a figurehead. In the United Kingdom the Prime Minister handles the affairs of the state, while the monarch (who is the head of state) has a largely ceremonial role with no political power. Russia also employs a similar structure, though the role of president has full political power. In Japan, there exists an emperor with little political power, with all government issues being handled by the prime minister. In Israel, while the Government is nominally a collegiate body with a primus inter pares role for the Prime Minister, the Israeli Prime Minister is the dominant figure in the executive branch in practice.


Assumption of power


Via election/appointment
Elections have been the usual mechanism by which representative government has operated since the 17th century.  However, in most parliamentary systems the prime minister is not directly elected by voters, but is the leader of the most dominant party in parliament. In presidential systems, the head of government is appointed by the president. According to Wolfgang Müller and Wilfried Philipp, heads of government have lasted in office on average 3.8 years in post-1945 Western Europe.


Seizure of power
In some instances, the head of government comes to political authority via force, such as in a coup. In authoritarian systems, the selection of the head of government is typically not open to the general public.
Under military dictatorships, the military’s leader usually fills the role of head of state, head of government, or both. A military dictator may install a figurehead as head of government, but generally keeps some or all executive governing powers for themselves.
grok_lead: The head of government is the chief executive official in a sovereign state or subnational polity, bearing primary responsibility for directing the executive branch, enforcing laws, and coordinating policy implementation to manage the practical affairs of governance. This role often entails operational leadership over ministries, budget execution, and crisis response, contrasting with the head of state, whose functions typically emphasize national symbolism, diplomatic representation, and unity beyond partisan divides. In systems featuring such a division, the head of government derives authority from legislative confidence or electoral mandate, enabling decisive action amid competing interests while the head of state remains above daily political contention. The configuration of the head of government varies by regime type: in presidential republics, such as the United States, the president concurrently holds both head of state and head of government positions, wielding unified executive authority including command of armed forces and veto power over legislation. In parliamentary systems, conversely, figures like prime ministers or chancellors lead the government as its head while answering to a legislature that can remove them via no-confidence votes, fostering accountability but risking instability from coalition dynamics. Semi-presidential arrangements, as in certain European states, blend elements by granting the president substantial powers alongside a prime ministerial head of government, which can lead to dual executive tensions during divided governance. These structural differences influence policy efficacy, with concentrated authority enabling swift decisions yet heightening risks of overreach, whereas diffused power promotes checks but may dilute responsiveness.
